hero.body:
The Indiantown Village Council voted Tuesday night to fire Village Manager Taryn Kryzda, who had been in the role since 2023, and appointed Michael Giardino as interim village manager during a meeting originally called to discuss a moratorium on data centers. Giardino was recently fired as Stuart city manager. The council also voted 4-1 to reject a proposed temporary pause on new large-scale data center applications and will instead seek a new legal opinion and lawsuit-proof language before taking action.

 Giardino said he was approached by two council members about the position and attended the special meeting where the council made its decision. He said it appeared to him that the voters wanted a change in Indiantown and that the village council received that information.

 Kimberly Jackson Brown, a 59-year resident of Indiantown, said the decision was a step in the right direction because the biggest change has to be to have the trust of the people for the council. She said if the village has a council that residents can trust, then all the changes can be enacted.

 The meeting addressed data centers, which has sparked debate within the community. After hearing public input, the council rejected a resolution to pause data center development and instructed its new legal counsel to revise the proposal's language. The data center issue will return to the council for further discussion.

The Indiantown Village Council voted Tuesday night to fire Village Manager Taryn Kryzda, who had held the position since 2023, and immediately appointed Michael Giardino as interim village manager during a meeting originally scheduled to address a proposed moratorium on data centers. Giardino, who was recently fired as Stuart city manager, told reporters he was approached by two council members about the position before the meeting. The abrupt leadership change comes as the village grapples with unfinished policy debates over data center development that have divided residents.

Giardino said two council members asked if he had an interest in the position and requested he attend the special meeting. Reflecting on the council's decision, Giardino said it appeared the voters wanted a change in Indiantown and the village council received that information and made a decision. Giardino said after hearing from residents and the village council at the meeting, he knows there is a difference to be made and hopes to be part of that.

Kimberly Jackson Brown, a 59-year resident of Indiantown, said the firing was a step in the right direction because the biggest change has to be to have the trust of the people for the council. Jackson Brown emphasized the importance of communication between the council and the community, saying residents understand they cannot get everything they want but want to be heard and informed when officials cannot deliver.

The council also rejected a resolution to pause data center development during Tuesday's meeting after hearing mixed public comment on the proposal. One resident said voting down data centers does not approve them but gives the community a chance to learn, while another warned officials they were messing with the wrong person when it comes to health concerns. The council instructed its new legal counsel to revise the proposal's language, and the data center issue will return to the council for further discussion.

A superseding indictment unsealed Wednesday charges Sherita Chandler of Port St. Lucie, along with defendants from Idaho, Illinois, California and Georgia, with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, making false claims and money laundering. Federal prosecutors allege the group worked from 2023 through 2024 to prepare and submit false individual and trust tax returns, along with more than 100 fictitious financial instruments, to claim refunds from the IRS. The defendants allegedly sought more than $57 million in refunds and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money, the Justice Department said.

 Chandler, Andrea and Kent Shannon of Kuna, Idaho, and Monika Skinger of Chicago had previously been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The Shannons also face additional allegations involving wire fraud, false claims and money laundering, including claims that they bought luxury vehicles with fraudulently obtained refunds. The investigation is being handled by IRS Criminal Investigation. A conspiracy to commit wire fraud charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City earlier this month have been legally surrendered by O'Donnell, clearing the way for adoptions. According to Martin County court records, O'Donnell hired an attorney and posted a surety bond following her not guilty plea. Sherita Chandler of Port St. Lucie is among seven people charged in an alleged tax refund fraud scheme that sought more than $57 million from the IRS, according to the U.S. Justice Department. A superseding indictment unsealed Wednesday charges Chandler, along with defendants from Idaho, Illinois, California and Georgia, with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, making false claims and money laundering.

Federal prosecutors allege the group worked from 2023 through 2024 to prepare and submit false individual and trust tax returns, along with more than 100 fictitious financial instruments, to claim refunds from the IRS. The defendants allegedly sought more than $57 million in refunds and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money, the Justice Department said.

Chandler, Andrea and Kent Shannon of Kuna, Idaho, and Monika Skinger of Chicago had previously been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, according to prosecutors. The Shannons also face additional allegations involving wire fraud, false claims and money laundering, including claims that they bought luxury vehicles with fraudulently obtained refunds. A conspiracy to commit wire fraud charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. All defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

Paige O'Donnell has pleaded not guilty to 72 charges stemming from what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case in its history, while legally surrendering the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home for adoption. O'Donnell hired an attorney and posted a surety bond following her not guilty plea, according to Martin County court records. The legal surrender clears the path for the rescued dogs to find new homes after undergoing medical evaluations and rehabilitation.

The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed O'Donnell's surrender of the dogs, saying staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations before placement decisions. The shelter will prepare the dogs for spay/neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside other animals in their care. Adoption applications are available on the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page, along with applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups.

The dogs were rescued from O'Donnell's hoarded Palm City home earlier this month after a WPTV investigation helped renew the Martin County Sheriff's Office probe into the case. Deputies found the animals living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, according to law enforcement, blaming strong odors on missed trash collection and old seafood.

Vero Beach police say they believe there are additional victims and expect more charges against a man accused of creating and sharing AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent. Police Chief David Currey said Thursday that the current eight charges against 37-year-old Peter Solomon Ruma involve one adult female victim. Ruma is being held at the Indian River County Jail on $1 million bond.

Ruma is charged with three counts of creating an altered sexual depiction, three counts of promoting an altered sexual depiction, one count of sexual cyber harassment and one count of cyberstalking. Investigators said the victim came forward after discovering her image had been altered. Detectives searched Ruma's home and seized two phones, and a forensic review of the devices produced evidence that advanced the investigation.

Police said Ruma allegedly used photographs of real women including images from social media and other publicly available online sources to make the altered sexual images. A person does not have to have sent an intimate photo to be victimized, police said. Currey said investigators have identified several other women who may have been subjected to similar conduct, some of whom may not know their images were obtained, manipulated or shared. The investigation uncovered complaints and law enforcement contacts involving unwanted communications and similar behavior dating back several years.

Ruma is employed as a Lyft driver and Uber Eats driver. Currey said investigators have not alleged criminal conduct occurred while Ruma was working for either service, but released the information as they seek potential victims or people with concerning interactions involving him. Police believe Ruma acted alone, though Currey said that could change as the investigation continues. Anyone who believes they may have been victimized, received altered or sexually explicit images from Ruma, or has information for detectives is asked to contact Vero Beach police Detective Greg Matakaitis at 772-978-4665.

More than a dozen Florida families have reported stolen SNAP benefits connected to a single address in Glendale, California. A majority of the purchases are for baby formula, which is known to be resold on the black market. After reaching out to DoorDash multiple times, the Tampa Bay 28 I-Team confirmed that nearly all of the purchases being made at the Glendale, California address are for baby formula.

 Victims described the financial toll of the theft. Shayna Houser Parra told the I-Team that she and her family still have not had all of their bills covered because of the theft. Cheyanne Smith said she has gone through three cards and that locks, canceling the card and changing her PIN have not worked.

 In July, one of the Florida victims posted the address the SNAP fraud is tied to in a Facebook group for DoorDash drivers in California. Someone responded, writing that they had delivered formula there like two or three times and each time it was like five to seven cans.

 The Glendale Police Department said it has received more calls from Florida law enforcement agencies since the I-Team's previous report, as its investigation continues. The Department of Children and Families has given no indication it is doing anything to investigate the fraud, instead directing people to contact law enforcement and increase the security on their accounts.

 Records show the U.S. Government Accountability Office also wanted to know what is being done to prevent SNAP benefit theft. However, there is no requirement for state agencies to report data on stolen benefits to the federal government. That authority ended in 2024, along with the Stolen SNAP Benefits Program that reimbursed victims of fraud, meaning the benefits stolen from families will not be returned.

Governor Ron DeSantis said Monday he will help persuade Floridians to approve Amendment 3, a property-tax proposal that would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. Under the amendment's ballot language, the expanded exemption would not apply to school district taxes.

 The proposal would also lower the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties, including businesses and rental properties, from 10 percent to 5 percent, and restrict how counties and municipalities use property-tax revenue. DeSantis said he has not settled on how he will participate and would not lead a political committee's statewide fundraising effort, but added he would be involved because he thinks the amendment is important.

 The governor rejected warnings from local leaders that the amendment would leave communities unable to provide basic services. DeSantis said he would support state funding to help rural counties with limited tax bases absorb revenue losses, though any state assistance would depend on lawmakers approving the funding. Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava launched a South Florida campaign Wednesday to defeat Amendment 3, joined by local leaders, labor organizations and business and civic groups. She warned that communities could face service cuts, higher fees or some combination of both, and said Miami-Dade could lose about 10 percent of its general fund revenue in the first year and 20 percent in the second.

 Levine Cava said renters and businesses could shoulder additional costs without receiving the expanded homestead exemption. Supporters have potentially encouraging polling numbers. A Sachs Media survey conducted August 18 randomly assigned 800 Florida voters to groups reviewing either the original ballot language or a court-ordered revision.

 Support was 65 percent among those who read the revised wording, compared with 60 percent among those who saw the original. The difference was not statistically significant.

 The Florida Policy Institute estimates that public hospital districts and health systems would lose approximately $323 million over three years under Amendment 3. The institute warns that reduced funding could affect staffing, access to care and programs serving uninsured and underinsured patients. Amendment 3 requires approval from at least 60 percent of voters casting ballots on the measure in November. If approved, it would take effect in January.

More than a dozen Florida families have reported stolen SNAP benefits connected to a single address in Glendale, California. A majority of the purchases are for baby formula, which is known to be resold on the black market. After reaching out to DoorDash multiple times, the Tampa Bay 28 I-Team confirmed that nearly all of the purchases being made at the Glendale, California address are for baby formula.

 Victims described the financial toll of the theft. Shayna Houser Parra told the I-Team that she and her family still have not had all of their bills covered because of the theft. Cheyanne Smith said she has gone through three cards and that locks, canceling the card and changing her PIN have not worked.

 In July, one of the Florida victims posted the address the SNAP fraud is tied to in a Facebook group for DoorDash drivers in California. Someone responded, writing that they had delivered formula there like two or three times and each time it was like five to seven cans.

 The Glendale Police Department said it has received more calls from Florida law enforcement agencies since the I-Team's previous report, as its investigation continues. The Department of Children and Families has given no indication it is doing anything to investigate the fraud, instead directing people to contact law enforcement and increase the security on their accounts.

 Records show the U.S. Government Accountability Office also wanted to know what is being done to prevent SNAP benefit theft. However, there is no requirement for state agencies to report data on stolen benefits to the federal government. That authority ended in 2024, along with the Stolen SNAP Benefits Program that reimbursed victims of fraud, meaning the benefits stolen from families will not be returned.

Governor Ron DeSantis said Monday he will help persuade Floridians to approve Amendment 3, a property-tax proposal that would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. Under the amendment's ballot language, the expanded exemption would not apply to school district taxes.

 The proposal would also lower the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties, including businesses and rental properties, from 10 percent to 5 percent, and restrict how counties and municipalities use property-tax revenue. DeSantis said he has not settled on how he will participate and would not lead a political committee's statewide fundraising effort, but added he would be involved because he thinks the amendment is important.

 The governor rejected warnings from local leaders that the amendment would leave communities unable to provide basic services. DeSantis said he would support state funding to help rural counties with limited tax bases absorb revenue losses, though any state assistance would depend on lawmakers approving the funding. Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava launched a South Florida campaign Wednesday to defeat Amendment 3, joined by local leaders, labor organizations and business and civic groups. She warned that communities could face service cuts, higher fees or some combination of both, and said Miami-Dade could lose about 10 percent of its general fund revenue in the first year and 20 percent in the second.

 Levine Cava said renters and businesses could shoulder additional costs without receiving the expanded homestead exemption. Supporters have potentially encouraging polling numbers. A Sachs Media survey conducted August 18 randomly assigned 800 Florida voters to groups reviewing either the original ballot language or a court-ordered revision.

 Support was 65 percent among those who read the revised wording, compared with 60 percent among those who saw the original. The difference was not statistically significant.

 The Florida Policy Institute estimates that public hospital districts and health systems would lose approximately $323 million over three years under Amendment 3. The institute warns that reduced funding could affect staffing, access to care and programs serving uninsured and underinsured patients. Amendment 3 requires approval from at least 60 percent of voters casting ballots on the measure in November. If approved, it would take effect in January.

State records show that over the past three years, former GOP communications director Taryn Fenske has secured more than $700,000 in government contracts through her PR company, TMF Communications. Fenske built her political career in Tallahassee, working for Governor Rick Scott, the Republican National Committee and Education Commissioner Richard Corcoran. By 2021, she was part of Governor Ron DeSantis' executive communications team and eventually worked for his presidential super PAC. After DeSantis' presidential run ended, Fenske launched her own private PR firm and state contract records show the DeSantis administration has been a steady client.

Since 2023, TMF Communications has been awarded five- and six-figure state contracts for PR consulting work across multiple agencies. Earlier this year, Florida's Department of Health allocated nearly $40,000 to TMF. In 2025, the Department of Children and Families budgeted $113,000 for TMF to support digital media vendors. In 2025, the Agency for Persons with Disabilities hired TMF to help rebrand the agency for $75,000. In 2026, another $52,000 was allocated to the TMF. Since 2023, New College has paid TMF more than $400,000 for PR consulting work. State contract records also show that in 2023, the state Justice Administration Commission paid TMF nearly $27,000 to assist with PR after Governor DeSantis suspended Orange County State Attorney Monique Worrell.

Ben Wilcox, who leads Integrity Florida, a nonpartisan government watchdog group, reviewed the findings and said that to the average citizen, the average taxpayer, that is an exorbitant amount of money. DeSantis' current communications director, Alex Lanfranconi, called TMF's state business awesome, describing Fenske as one of the best communications professionals in the state. Fenske declined to speak on camera. In an email, she called the premise of a question over whether her loyalty to the DeSantis administration contributed to her state work insulting and dismissive of her professional qualifications. She also said her company's work was earned on its merits.

DCF recommends SNAP recipients visit a Department Family Resource Center to add a security code to their account, which families in contact with the I-Team say has been effective.

hero.body:
Paige O'Donnell has pleaded not guilty to 72 charges stemming from what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case in its history, while legally surrendering the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home for adoption. According to Martin County court records, O'Donnell hired an attorney and posted a surety bond following her not guilty plea. The legal surrender clears the path for the rescued dogs to find new homes after undergoing medical evaluations and rehabilitation.

The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed O'Donnell's surrender of the dogs, saying staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations before placement decisions. Potential adopters will receive clear information about any long-term medical needs the animals may have. The shelter will prepare the dogs for spay/neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside other animals in their care. Adoption applications are available on the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page, along with applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups. The shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time to keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services.

The dogs were rescued from O'Donnell's hoarded Palm City home earlier this month after a WPTV investigation helped renew the Martin County Sheriff's Office probe into the case. Deputies found the animals living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, according to law enforcement, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood." The rescued Border Collies underwent what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process involving carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said the shelter shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine. Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur.

Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions. "As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down." The case has prompted legislative action from State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, who is pushing for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is encouraging the public to adopt or foster available animals while the rescued Border Collies continue receiving treatment and rehabilitation.

Investigators determined that Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. Aug. 27, and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed that his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge.

On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to a body. Budensiek said investigators had not officially confirmed whether the body was Debevec's, but the deceased person was wearing clothing matching what Debevec was believed to have been wearing. Debevec's family was notified that a body was found.

Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office are investigating a shootout between two teenagers, ages 15 and 17, in a residential neighborhood Wednesday night. The incident occurred in the 1100 block of 12th Court Southwest at around 7:30 p.m. Deputies responded to multiple 911 calls and found bullet casings at the scene. A nearby home and vehicle had been struck by gunfire.

 Investigators said they obtained video showing the two teenagers shooting at each other in the roadway. Kevin Jaworski, a spokesman for the sheriff's office, confirmed the exchange. Authorities released a photo of one of the weapons believed to have been used in the shooting.

 Jaworski said the weapon was recovered after the 17-year-old suspect was taken into custody Thursday morning. The weapon was described as a short-barreled pistol rifle.

 Authorities believe the shootout stemmed from an ongoing feud between the two teens. While the cause of the feud remains unclear, officials said the incident appears to be isolated. Jaworski said the shooting was between the two juveniles and there is no threat to the community at this point, but noted it is inherently dangerous to be shooting firearms in the middle of the street because a car was hit and a house was hit, and anyone in those locations could have easily been hurt.

 Neighbors said detectives were in the area throughout the night gathering evidence, and everyone is relieved no one was injured. Julio Pitts, a resident in the area, said he was sitting in his living room when the shots rang out. The case remains under investigation, and authorities are urging anyone with information to contact detectives.

Chavi Rose-Marie Hammock, 23, of Vero Beach was arrested Aug. 28 on an active warrant charging her with grand theft and uttering a forged instrument after law enforcement in New York reported that two checks had allegedly been altered and deposited into a TD Bank account belonging to Hammock, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Investigators said one of the checks was changed from $800 to $17,658 before it was deposited.

Bank records showed deposits totaling $37,316 were made into Hammock's account in October 2024, detectives said. Cash withdrawals followed, including a withdrawal of $16,500, before the account was later closed, investigators allege. Surveillance images and video provided by TD Bank appeared to show Hammock conducting transactions connected to the deposits and withdrawals, according to the warrant affidavit, and a witness later identified Hammock from surveillance photos.

Authorities allege the transactions occurred between October and November 2024 and resulted in more than $37,000 being obtained through fraudulent means. Hammock was booked into the Indian River County Jail and the case remains under investigation.

hero.body:
A Vero Beach man arrested Wednesday on eight charges for creating and distributing AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without consent is expected to face additional charges as investigators believe more victims have yet to be identified. Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, is being held at the Indian River County Jail on $1 million bond after his arrest on charges stemming from incidents occurring between June and August 2026 involving one adult female victim. Police Chief David Currey said Thursday that investigators have identified several other women who may have been subjected to similar conduct, some of whom may not know their images were obtained, manipulated or shared.

 Ruma faces three counts of creating an altered sexual depiction, three counts of promoting an altered sexual depiction, one count of sexual cyber harassment and one count of cyberstalking. The victim came forward after discovering her image had been altered. Detectives searched Ruma's home and seized two phones, and a forensic review of the devices produced evidence that advanced the investigation.

 Police said Ruma allegedly used photographs of real women, including images from social media and other publicly available online sources, to make the altered sexual images. A person does not have to have sent an intimate photo to be victimized, police said.

 Ruma is employed as a Lyft driver and Uber Eats driver. Currey stressed that investigators have not alleged criminal conduct occurred while Ruma was working for either service, but released the information as they seek potential victims or people with concerning interactions involving him. Police also said the investigation uncovered complaints and law enforcement contacts involving unwanted communications and similar behavior dating back several years.

 Anyone who believes they may have been victimized, received altered or sexually explicit images from Ruma, or has information for detectives is asked to contact Vero Beach police Detective Greg Matakaitis at 772-978-4665.
